hook.text: A franchisor pushes a failing franchisee out, collects a new franchise fee from the replacement, and repeats.

buildup.text: Churning is when franchisors profit from turnover: each new owner pays fresh fees on the same location.

discovery.text: The franchisor wins regardless: franchise fees from the new buyer, royalties from whoever is operating.

twist.text: Some franchise systems have 50%+ turnover over 5 years, hidden behind new openings that mask closures.

climax.text: Churning extracts value from aspiring entrepreneurs. The location profits the franchisor, not the operator.

punchline.text: New owner, same store, fresh fees. Churning profits the franchisor every time.

quiz.question: What is franchise churning?
options: Profiting from repeated ownership turnover at locations

details.summary: Franchise churning occurs when a franchisor terminates or does not renew a franchisee's agreement, repurchases or reassigns the location, and collects a new franchise fee from the replacement operator..
details.whyItMatters: Churning reveals how franchisors can profit from franchisee turnover rather than franchisee success. High churn rates signal systemic problems in the franchise system and should be a red flag for prospective franchise buyers reviewing FDD data.
takeaways: Franchisors collect new franchise fees each time a location changes operators
High turnover rates in the FDD signal potential churning or systemic profitability issues
Churning extracts value from established locations at the expense of departing franchisees

faq.question: How can prospective franchisees identify churning in the FDD?
faq.answer: Item 20 of the FDD lists franchise transfers, terminations, and non-renewals over the past three years. High termination rates, frequent transfers, and a pattern of short franchise lifespans indicate potential churning. Contact former franchisees listed in the FDD for their perspective.

faq.question: What protections exist against franchise churning?
faq.answer: Some states have franchise relationship laws requiring good cause for termination and rights of first refusal. Strong franchisee associations lobby against churning practices. Documenting compliance meticulously protects against pretextual termination..
